The Lancet GRAM study confirms the figures in your query. It estimated 1.14 million deaths directly attributable to bacterial AMR in 2021, and forecasts about 39 million direct AMR deaths from 2025 to 2050.

- **2021 baseline:** Reports agree that 1.14 million direct deaths occurred in 2021, with 4.71 million deaths associated with bacterial AMR in the same year. (The associated figure includes deaths where AMR was a contributing factor.)

- **Regional and age patterns:** South Asia is forecast to have the highest totals, with 11.8 million direct AMR deaths between 2025 and 2050. Among older adults, deaths among people 70 years and older are projected to more than double by 2050, while child deaths under five are projected to halve.

The study was published in The Lancet as "Global burden of bacterial antimicrobial resistance 1990–2021: a systematic analysis with forecasts to 2050," and covers 204 countries and territories.

# HTB26 **Resistance-aware antibiotic prioritisation: which approved drugs are still worth trying against a resistant bacterium, and why.** Built for Hack The Burgh 2026. ## The problem Antibiotic resistance is a slow-moving pandemic, and the drugs we rely on are running out faster than they are being replaced. - Bacterial antimicrobial resistance (AMR) was directly responsible for an estimated **1.14 million deaths in 2021** and associated with **4.71 million**. The Lancet's Global Burden of Disease forecast puts the toll at **39 million direct deaths between 2025 and 2050** ([Lancet GRAM study, via Oxford Population Health](https://www.ndm.ox.ac.uk/news/antibiotic-resistance-could-cause-39-million-deaths-between-now-and-2050)). - The WHO's 2024 priority list places carbapenem-resistant *Acinetobacter baumannii* and carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales, which includes *Klebsiella pneumoniae*, in its **critical** tier ([WHO Bacterial Priority Pathogens List 2024](https://www.news-medical.net/news/20240520/WHO-updates-Bacterial-Priority-Pathogens-List-to-combat-antimicrobial-resistance.aspx)). - The pipeline is thin and shrinking. WHO counts **90 antibacterials in clinical development, down from 97 in 2023**, and only **15** are considered innovative. Just 17 new agents against priority pathogens have been approved since 2017, and only two are a genuinely new chemical class ([WHO, 2025](https://www.who.int/news/item/02-10-2025-who-releases-new-reports-on-new-tests-and-treatments-in-development-for-bacterial-infections)). New antibiotics take a decade or more to reach patients. In the meantime, clinicians and researchers need a faster way to ask a narrower question: **given what this isolate is resistant to, which drugs we already have are least likely to be defeated?** ## What we built A researcher-facing tool that takes a pathogen, or a set of resistance genes, and: 1. **Maps resistance.** Resistance determinants are linked to their mechanisms and the drug classes they affect, using the CARD database. 2. **Ranks approved antibiotics.** Each candidate is scored on whether the isolate's mechanisms are known to defeat it, so the shortlist favours drugs that evade the resistance in play. 3. **Shows its working.** Every ranking comes with a plain-language explanation, cited activity evidence and recorded property checks, so a researcher can audit the reasoning rather than trust a black box. We focus on three high-burden pathogens: *Staphylococcus aureus*, *Klebsiella pneumoniae* and *Acinetobacter baumannii*. A second, discovery-oriented track extends the same framework towards whole-cell screening for novel *A. baumannii* candidates, with generated molecules kept strictly separate from approved drugs. ## Why it is credible - **Honest by design.** The tool proposes which drugs are *not known to be defeated*. It does not claim that a drug will cure anything, and nothing here is clinical or dosing advice. - **Validated against real data.** The ranking rule was pre-registered and tested against measured susceptibility results from over 5,000 isolates. It beats chance overall, and we report plainly where it does not beat a simple drug-and-species baseline. - **Reproducible and offline-capable.** The demo runs from saved data with no external services, and clearly labels anything illustrative. ## Pipeline Solid arrows show the working demo path; dashed arrows show planned extensions. ```mermaid flowchart TD P["Pathogen presets"] --> C["Saved CARD resistance profiles"] C --> R["Evasion ranking
approved drugs per pathogen
activity evidence"] R --> S["Recorded property checks"] S --> U["Researcher view
resistance map, shortlist, explanations and caveats"] G["Typed resistance genes"] --> CP["Computed resistance profile"] CP -.-> R F["Illustrative MRSA fixture
labelled on screen"] --> U subgraph W [Planned whole-cell discovery: A. baumannii] D["Labelled data and retrieval library"] -.-> L["Leakage-controlled splits"] L -.-> M["Activity ensemble"] M -.-> N["Candidate generation"] N -.-> Q["Filter cascade"] Q -.-> O["Oracle interface and cost ledger"] O -.-> V["Hidden-drug evaluation and baselines"] O -.-> A["Scheduler and calibrated explanations"] end V -.-> U A -.-> U U -.-> B["Cited browser verification"] T["Ground truth and pre-run protocol"] -.-> E["Retrospective results with intervals"] E -.-> R ``` ## Impact Resistance data is abundant; the bottleneck is turning it into a decision a researcher can act on and defend. By making the reasoning transparent and the limits explicit, this tool helps teams narrow a large drug space to a short, evidenced list, and points the way towards finding the next generation of antibiotics. See [docs/limits.md](docs/limits.md) for a full account of what the tool does and does not claim, and [THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md](THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md) for data sources and reused code.

Written for: hackathon judges and general technical readers.

**README**

The pitch README and the deletion of `scope.md` and `tasks.md` are committed on `main` as `c929204`. I haven't pushed it.

- **Stash:** I stashed the changes on `login`, switched to `main`, and applied them there.
- **Pull first:** Local `main` was 12 commits behind `origin/main`, so I fast-forwarded it before applying. Otherwise the commit would have been on a stale base.
- **README conflict:** `origin/main` had renamed the title to "NovaBiotech" and added a link to the Boltz guide at the bottom. I kept the new pitch, used "NovaBiotech" as its title, and dropped the Boltz link as codebase-specific. Tell me if you want it back.
- **`.DS_Store`:** It had been picked up in the stash. I unstaged it, so it isn't in the commit, and it's still untracked.
- **Stash entries:** I left `stash@{0}` (this change) in place as a backup. The permission check refused my attempt to drop it, so drop it with `git stash drop` once you're happy. The older `autostash` and `WS3 uncommitted work` entries were already there, and I didn't touch them.

The `login` branch still has its original, un-pitched version of these edits only in the stash, since I didn't commit them there.
